concepts.name: Hidden struct copies from readonly members and readonly fields
Kafka offset commit timing: at-most-once vs at-least-once

choices.text: 1, because `Increment` updates `_n` before it is read
0, because `Increment` runs on a hidden copy of `c`
Nothing: a `readonly` member can't call `Increment`
1 on the first call, then 0 once the copy is cached

questions.explanation: A `readonly` member promises not to change the struct, yet it may call a non-`readonly` member. To keep the promise, the compiler copies the struct and calls `Increment` on the copy, so the original `_n` stays 0 and 0 is printed. It compiles (with a warning), so the 'can't call' answer is wrong. Mark `Increment`-free members `readonly`, or make the whole struct a `readonly struct`, to avoid these hidden copies.

sources.title: Structure types - C# reference
sources.claim: A readonly instance member can call a non-readonly member; the compiler then creates a copy of the structure instance and calls the non-readonly member on that copy, so the original instance isn't modified.

questions.prompt: A Kafka consumer reads a batch, commits its offsets straight away, and then processes the messages. It crashes halfway through the batch and restarts. What happens to the messages it hadn't processed?

choices.text: Redelivered, because Kafka tracks an acknowledgement for each message
Skipped, because the committed position is already past them
Redelivered, because the crash rolls the committed offset back
Moved to a dead-letter topic when the consumer group rebalances

questions.explanation: A Kafka consumer's progress is just its saved position in the partition log, not a per-message acknowledgement. Saving the position before processing gives at-most-once delivery: after a crash the consumer resumes from the saved position, so the unprocessed messages are never seen again. Processing first and saving the position afterwards gives at-least-once delivery instead, with possible duplicates. Kafka has no built-in dead-letter topic.

sources.title: Design (Apache Kafka documentation)
sources.claim: If the consumer saves its position and then processes the messages, a crash in between means the next consumer starts from the saved position and some messages are never processed (at-most-once); processing first and then saving the position gives at-least-once, with possible reprocessing after a crash.

questions.prompt: Ops wants to install only the .NET 10 runtime on new servers and keep deploying your framework-dependent `net8.0` services there unchanged. Will the services start? Explain why, and give your options.

model_answer.summary: Not by default: a framework-dependent app rolls forward to a newer patch or minor version of its own major version, never to a new major, so a `net8.0` app won't start where only .NET 10 is installed. Install the .NET 8 runtime, deploy self-contained, retarget to `net10.0`, or opt in to major roll-forward after testing.
key_points: The default roll-forward policy is `Minor`: the host uses the latest installed patch of the requested major.minor, or a higher minor of the same major, but never a higher major, so the app fails to start

You can opt in with a `RollForward` value such as `Major` or `LatestMajor` (project property, `runtimeconfig.json`, `DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD` or `--roll-forward`), but only after testing on .NET 10, since behaviour can differ
Safer options are installing the .NET 8 runtime side by side, publishing self-contained so the app carries its own runtime, or retargeting the services to `net10.0`

questions.explanation: Many people assume the newest runtime runs everything, as with .NET Framework 4.x in-place updates. Modern .NET runtimes are side by side: the host only rolls a framework-dependent app forward within its major version unless you change the `RollForward` policy. A self-contained deployment picks its runtime at publish time, so it doesn't depend on what the server has installed.

sources.title: Select which .NET version to use
sources.claim: A framework-dependent app uses the latest installed patch of its requested version, or rolls forward to a higher minor version (the default Minor policy) but not to a lower or higher major; RollForward can be set in the project, runtimeconfig.json, DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD or --roll-forward to values such as Major or LatestMajor; self-contained deployments include the runtime selected at publish time.

choices.text: 1, 2 and 3, since the field is updated where it lives
0 each time: each call increments a temporary copy
Nothing: a `readonly` field can't call `Increment`
1 and then it throws, since the field can't change

questions.explanation: Outside a constructor, a `readonly` field of a struct type is a value, not a variable. Calling a method on a value makes the compiler copy it into a temporary and call the method on the temporary, so `Increment` changes the copy and `_counter` stays 0. Nothing fails to compile or throws: the bug is silent. Make the struct immutable (`readonly struct`), or drop `readonly` from the field if it must mutate.

sources.title: Expressions - C# language specification
sources.claim: If a field is readonly and the reference occurs outside an instance constructor, the result is a value rather than a variable (§12.8.4); when a function member is invoked on a value of a value type, a temporary local variable is created, so modifications made to `this` don't affect the original (§12.6.6).

sources.title: readonly keyword - C# reference
sources.claim: Because value types directly contain their data, a field that is a readonly value type is immutable.

questions.prompt: To stop losing messages, a team changes its Kafka consumer to process each batch first and commit the offsets only afterwards. What must the handler now cope with?

choices.text: Lost messages, whenever it crashes before the commit runs
Duplicates, as a crash before the commit replays it
Out-of-order messages within a partition after late commits
The producer resending every message not yet committed

questions.explanation: Processing before saving the position is at-least-once delivery. If the consumer crashes after processing but before committing, it restarts from the old position and processes those messages again, so the handler must be idempotent. Nothing is lost, order within a partition is unchanged, and the producer isn't involved: the position belongs to the consumer.

sources.title: Design (Apache Kafka documentation)
sources.claim: If the consumer reads, processes and then saves its position, a crash after processing but before saving means the new consumer reprocesses some messages: at-least-once delivery.

questions.prompt: A framework-dependent app targets `net8.0` with default settings. The server has the .NET runtimes 8.0.5, 8.0.11 and 10.0.2 installed. Which one does it run on?

choices.text: 10.0.2, because the host always picks the newest runtime
8.0.5, because the host binds to the lowest match it finds
8.0.11, the latest patch of the requested major and minor
None: it needs the exact patch it was compiled against

questions.explanation: When the requested major.minor (8.0) is installed, the host uses its highest installed patch, so security fixes apply without rebuilding. It doesn't jump to a new major (10.0) unless you opt in with a `RollForward` policy such as `LatestMajor`, and it doesn't require the exact patch: only `Disable` does that, which is meant for testing.

sources.title: Select which .NET version to use
sources.claim: The host chooses the latest patch version installed for the requested version (the default Minor policy uses LatestPatch when the requested minor is present); major roll-forward needs Major or LatestMajor, and Disable binds only to the specified version.
